title: Moses, Exodus and Sinai
objective: After this level you can retell the Exodus as Jews tell it, explain the giving of the Torah at Sinai, and say what historians can and cannot confirm.
summary: Moses led the Israelites out of Egyptian slavery to Sinai, where Jews believe God gave the Torah. Archaeology has not confirmed the story; Israel is first named about 1205 BCE.

cards.headline: It is the story Jews retell at every Passover meal.
cards.body: Slaves walk out of Egypt, and at a mountain in the desert they receive a law. Here is the story as the Bible tells it, what it means to Jews, and what historians can and can't say about it.

cards.headline: Out of Egypt
cards.body: In the biblical account, a pharaoh enslaved the Hebrews in Egypt. After a series of plagues struck the land, he let them go, and Moses led them through the Red Sea, which, the Bible says, God parted for them. No wonder Jewish tradition reveres Moses as its greatest prophet and teacher.

cards.headline: A law that begins with a rescue
cards.body: At Mount Sinai, the Bible tells, God made the Israelites his people and gave them the terms of his covenant, including the Ten Commandments. Notice how they open: "I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." The law starts by recalling a rescue. Many Jews also hold that an Oral Torah, laws and customs passed down by word of mouth, was revealed to Moses.

cards.headline: What historians can say
cards.body: Archaeology has not confirmed the Exodus as the Bible describes it. The Bible scholar S. David Sperling notes there is no archaeological evidence that the Israelites were ever in Egypt. The earliest widely accepted mention of Israel is an inscription of the pharaoh Merneptah from about 1205 BCE. Some historians still think an escape by part of Israel's ancestors lies behind the story, given how central it became to Israel's faith.

cards.headline: Moses, Exodus and Sinai: the takeaways
learned: The Bible tells how Moses led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt
At Sinai, Jews believe, God gave the covenant's law, starting with the Ten Commandments
Archaeology has not confirmed the Exodus; Israel is first named about 1205 BCE

questions.prompt: Whose inscription, from about 1205 BCE, holds the earliest widely accepted mention of Israel?

options.label: Moses himself, on the tablets from Sinai
The Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II
options.rationale: He lived about six centuries later.

options.label: The Persian king Cyrus the Great

questions.explanation: An inscription of the pharaoh Merneptah, from about 1205 BCE, is the earliest widely accepted mention of Israel.

questions.prompt: The Ten Commandments open by naming God as the one who brought Israel out of Egypt. What does that show?

options.label: That the commandments were written in Egypt
options.rationale: They were given at Sinai, after the Exodus.

options.label: That only Egyptians had to obey them
options.rationale: They were given to the Israelites.

options.label: That the covenant law starts from the rescue from slavery
That the Exodus is proven by archaeology

questions.explanation: The law opens by recalling the rescue "out of the house of bondage": the covenant rests on it.

questions.prompt: Level 3 used the Passover meal to show two dimensions working together. Which story does that meal retrace?

options.label: The Exodus from Egypt, joining ritual and story
Abraham's journey from Ur, joining doctrine and ethics
The building of the Temple, joining material and law
The creation of the world, joining experience and doctrine

questions.explanation: As Jews share the Passover meal they retrace the Exodus, binding ritual and narrative together.
